claim: Transcription by RNA polymerase II requires assembly of a preinitiation complex (PIC) composed of general transcription factors (GTFs) bound at the promoter.
source: Transcription by RNA polymerase II requires assembly of a preinitiation complex (PIC) composed of general transcription factors (GTFs) bound at the promoter.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about transcription that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In vitro, some GTFs are essential for transcription, whereas others are not required under certain conditions.
source: In vitro, some GTFs are essential for transcription, whereas others are not required under certain conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research throughout the manuscript.

claim: PICs are stable in the absence of nucleotide triphosphates.
source: PICs are stable in the absence of nucleotide triphosphates
evidence: This is supported by references to prior in vitro studies cited in the manuscript (Conaway and Conaway, 1993; Buratowski, 1994; Orphanides et al., 1996; Roeder, 1996).

claim: Subsets of GTFs can form partial PICs in vitro.
source: subsets of GTFs can form partial PICs
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research (Buratowski et al., 1989).

claim: All GTFs are essential for TBP binding and transcription in vivo.
source: By depleting individual GTFs in yeast cells, we show that all GTFs are essential for TBP binding and transcription
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GTF depletion experiments shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Partial PICs do not exist at appreciable levels in vivo.
source: suggesting that partial PICs do not exist at appreciable levels in vivo
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TBP occupancy is drastically reduced upon depletion of any individual GTF (Figure 4).

claim: Depletion of FACT strongly reduces PIC formation and transcription.
source: Depletion of FACT, a histone chaperone that travels with elongating Pol II, strongly reduces PIC formation and transcription.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: FACT is a histone chaperone that travels with elongating Pol II.
source: FACT, a histone chaperone that travels with elongating Pol II
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript (Mason and Struhl, 2003).

claim: TAFs contribute to transcription of most genes.
source: TAFs contribute to transcription of most genes
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: TAF-independent transcription occurs at substantial levels, preferentially at promoters containing TATA elements.
source: TAF-independent transcription occurs at substantial levels, preferentially at promoters containing TATA elements
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: PICs are absent in cells deprived of uracil.
source: PICs are absent in cells deprived of uracil, and presumably UTP
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Transcriptionally inactive PICs are removed from promoters in vivo.
source: suggesting that transcriptionally inactive PICs are removed from promoters in vivo
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PICs are absent in uracil-deprived cells (Figure 5).

claim: GTFs were defined originally as factors necessary and sufficient for 'basal' transcription from core promoters in vitro.
source: GTFs were defined originally as factors necessary and sufficient for 'basal' transcription from core promoters in vitro.
evidence: This is a historical statement about the field supported by established knowledge.

claim: TFIIA is dispensable or only mildly stimulatory under some in vitro conditions.
source: However, TFIIA is dispensable or only mildly stimulatory under other conditions (Ozer et al., 1994; Sun et al., 1994; Yokomori et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TFIIE, TFIIF, and TFIIH can be dispensable or only stimulatory for transcription from negatively-supercoiled templates, depending on the promoter.
source: TFIIE, TFIIF, and TFIIH can be dispensable or only stimulatory for transcription from negatively-supercoiled templates, depending on the promoter (Parvin and Sharp, 1993; Goodrich and Tjian, 1994; Parvin et al., 1994; Timmers, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TBP-independent transcription that requires only YY1, TFIIB, and Pol II has been observed on supercoiled templates with the YYI initiation element.
source: TBP-independent transcription that requires only YY1, TFIIB, and Pol II has been observed on supercoiled templates with the YYI initiation element (Usheva and Shenk, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The PIC is a stable entity that initiates transcription upon addition of nucleotide triphosphates in vitro.
source: In vitro, the PIC is a stable entity that initiates transcription upon addition of nucleotide triphosphates (Conaway and Conaway, 1993; Buratowski, 1994; Orphanides et al., 1996; Roeder, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PIC assembly is initiated with the binding of TBP (or the TFIID complex) to the promoter.
source: PIC assembly is initiated with the binding of TBP (or the TFIID complex) to the promoter, as none of the other factors can stably bind DNA on their own (Buratowski et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: None of the GTFs other than TBP can stably bind DNA on their own.
source: as none of the other factors can stably bind DNA on their own (Buratowski et al., 1989)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: GTFs can be sequentially added to give a series of stable, 'partial PICs' prior to assembly of a transcriptionally active PIC in vitro.
source: GTFs can be sequentially added to give a series of stable, 'partial PICs' prior to assembly of a transcriptionally active PIC (Buratowski et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Structures of functional PICs have been determined at the atomic level.
source: structures of functional PICs have now been determined at the atomic level (Sainsbury et al., 2015; Robinson et al., 2016; Hantsche and Cramer, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Functional PICs can vary with respect to the presence or absence of TAFs, Mediator, and TFIIA.
source: Functional PICs can vary with respect to the presence or absence of TAFs, Mediator, and TFIIA.
evidence: This is supported by prior research and structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: TBP, TFIIB, and Pol II are essential for transcription in vivo.
source: Depletion studies indicate that TBP, TFIIB, and Pol II are essential for transcription (Moqtaderi et al., 1996; Fan et al., 2010; Wong et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TFIIA is important but not essential for transcription in vivo according to prior studies.
source: whereas TFIIA is important but not essential (Chou et al., 1999; Liu et al., 1999; Stargell et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research, though the manuscript later challenges this conclusion.

claim: The kinase subunit of TFIIH (Kin28) is important for promoter escape and Mediator dissociation.
source: The kinase subunit of TFIIH (Kin28) is important for promoter escape and Mediator dissociation, but considerable transcription occurs upon its depletion or inactivation (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Considerable transcription occurs upon Kin28 depletion or inactivation.
source: but considerable transcription occurs upon its depletion or inactivation (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Depletion of the entire Mediator complex abolishes Pol II transcription.
source: Depletion of the entire Mediator complex abolishes Pol II transcription, but Mediator sub-modules can support transcription, albeit at lower levels than the wild-type strain, and can inhibit promoter escape (Petrenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mediator sub-modules can support transcription at lower levels than the wild-type strain.
source: but Mediator sub-modules can support transcription, albeit at lower levels than the wild-type strain, and can inhibit promoter escape (Petrenko et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mediator sub-modules can inhibit promoter escape.
source: and can inhibit promoter escape (Petrenko et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Most studies indicate that Taf1 has a selective role at TATA-less promoters.
source: Most studies indicate a selective role at TATA-less promoters (Moqtaderi et al., 1996; Kuras et al., 2000; Li et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some studies suggest a general requirement for Taf1 in Pol II transcription.
source: whereas others suggest a general requirement for Pol II transcription (Warfield et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The relative occupancies of GTFs at promoters are consistent across all promoters.
source: The relative occupancies of GTFs at promoters are consistent across all promoters (Kuras et al., 2000; Pokholok et al., 2002; Rhee and Pugh, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A structurally similar PIC mediates a given level of transcription at all promoters.
source: strongly suggesting that a structurally similar PIC mediates a given level of transcription
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GTF occupancies are consistent across promoters.

claim: Mediator occupancy at core promoters is transient, due to Kin28-dependent dissociation.
source: Mediator occupancy at core promoters is transient, due to Kin28-dependent dissociation, but it is strongly correlated with GTF occupancies upon Kin28 depletion (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mediator occupancy is strongly correlated with GTF occupancies upon Kin28 depletion.
source: but it is strongly correlated with GTF occupancies upon Kin28 depletion (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mediator stimulates PIC formation but is not an obligate component of the PIC in vivo.
source: Nevertheless, while Mediator stimulates PIC formation, it is not an obligate component of the PIC in vivo (Petrenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: TAF occupancy does not strictly correlate with GTF occupancy.
source: TAF occupancy does not strictly correlate with GTF occupancy, providing strong evidence that transcription can be mediated by TAF-containing (i.e. TFIID) and TAF-lacking forms of transcriptionally active TBP, with the relative usage of these two forms depending on the promoter (Kuras et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Transcription can be mediated by TAF-containing (TFIID) and TAF-lacking forms of transcriptionally active TBP.
source: providing strong evidence that transcription can be mediated by TAF-containing (i.e. TFIID) and TAF-lacking forms of transcriptionally active TBP, with the relative usage of these two forms depending on the promoter (Kuras et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The relative usage of TAF-containing and TAF-lacking TBP forms depends on the promoter.
source: with the relative usage of these two forms depending on the promoter (Kuras et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Promoters can be classified as either constitutive, TATA-lacking, and TFIID-dependent or inducible, TATA-containing, TFIID-independent, and SAGA-dependent.
source: Depending on which TBP form predominates, promoters can be classified roughly as either 1) constitutive, TATA-lacking, and TFIID-dependent or 2) inducible, TATA-containing, TFIID-independent, and SAGA-dependent (Struhl, 1986; Chen and Struhl, 1988; Struhl, 1987; Iyer and Struhl, 1995; Moqtaderi et al., 1996; Basehoar et al., 2004; Huisinga and Pugh, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The TFIID form is specifically recruited by the Rap1-containing activator and associated NuA4 histone acetylase complex to promoters of ribosomal protein genes.
source: First, the TFIID form is specifically recruited by the Rap1-containing activator and associated NuA4 histone acetylase complex to promoters of ribosomal protein genes (Li et al., 2002; Mencía et al., 2002; Uprety et al., 2012; Uprety et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many activators do not directly recruit TFIID but rather recruit the SAGA histone acetylase complex.
source: In contrast, many other activators do not directly recruit TFIID (Kuras et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000) but rather recruit the SAGA histone acetylase complex (Bhaumik and Green, 2001; Bhaumik et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TBP is preferentially retained at TAF-containing vs TAF-lacking promoters upon thermal inactivation of TFIIB or Mediator.
source: Second, TBP is preferentially retained at the TAF-containing vs TAF-lacking promoters upon thermal inactivation of TFIIB or Mediator (Li et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The relative use of TFIID- vs. SAGA-dependent mechanisms at a given promoter can differ depending on the environmental conditions.
source: Third, the relative use of TFIID- vs. SAGA-dependent mechanisms at a given promoter can differ depending on the environmental conditions (Ferdoush et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Growth of anchor-away strains is comparable to that of an untagged parental strain in the absence of rapamycin.
source: In the absence of rapamycin, growth of these strains is comparable to that of an untagged parental strain (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fusion of the FRB domain to the targeted factors does not significantly affect their function.
source: indicating that the fusion of the FRB domain to the targeted factors does not significantly affect their function
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that growth is comparable to wild-type in the absence of rapamycin (Figure 1A).

claim: Anchor-away strains fail to grow when GTFs are removed from the nucleus by treatment with rapamycin.
source: In contrast, when these proteins are removed from the nucleus by treatment with rapamycin, these strains fail to grow (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Binding of the targeted GTFs at active promoters is reduced to background or near-background levels after rapamycin treatment for 1 hr.
source: Binding of the targeted GTFs at active promoters (PMA1 and CCW12) is reduced to background or near-background levels after rapamycin treatment for 1 hr (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Depletion of GTFs is highly effective.
source: indicating that depletion of GTFs is highly effective
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GTF binding is reduced to background levels after rapamycin treatment (Figure 1B).

claim: Addition of rapamycin has minimal effects on transcription in an untagged parental control strain.
source: While the addition of rapamycin has minimal effects on transcription in an untagged parental control strain
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pol II occupancy at coding regions of all genes tested is reduced to very low levels upon depletion of any GTF.
source: Pol II occupancy at coding regions of all genes tested is reduced to very low levels upon depletion of any GTF (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of any GTF drastically reduced transcription to near-background levels as determined by metagene or individual gene analyses.
source: In all cases, depletion of any GTF drastically reduced transcription to near-background levels as determined by metagene (Figure 2A) or individual gene (Figure 2B) analyses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Depletion of Taf1 results in a modest decrease in transcription.
source: In contrast, as will be discussed later, depletion of Taf1 results in a modest decrease in transcription.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Upon TBP depletion, TBP and Pol II occupancies decrease in a kinetically similar manner.
source: Furthermore, upon TBP depletion, TBP and Pol II occupancies decrease in a kinetically similar manner (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Loss of TBP results in an immediate cessation of transcriptional initiation.
source: indicating that loss of TBP results in an immediate cessation of transcriptional initiation
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TBP and Pol II occupancies decrease in a kinetically similar manner upon TBP depletion (Figure 2C).

claim: Induction of HSP12 is very strongly decreased upon depletion of all GTFs (but not Taf1).
source: In accord with drastic transcriptional effects described on non-inducible genes, induction of HSP12 (Figure 3A) and other heat shock genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) is very strongly decreased, although not completely eliminated, for all GTFs (but not Taf1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Induction of heat shock genes is not completely eliminated upon GTF depletion.
source: is very strongly decreased, although not completely eliminated, for all GTFs (but not Taf1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The anchor-away system works somewhat less efficiently in stress conditions.
source: In this regard, the anchor-away system works somewhat less efficiently in stress conditions (Petrenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Incomplete depletion of an essential GTF will reduce (but not eliminate) transcription and its occupancy at the promoter, but it will not affect the nature of the PIC and hence the GTF:Pol II occupancy ratio.
source: As discussed and shown elsewhere for TBP (Petrenko et al., 2017), incomplete depletion of an essential GTF will reduce (but not eliminate) transcription and its occupancy at the promoter, but it will not affect the nature of the PIC and hence the GTF:Pol II occupancy ratio.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and logical inference.

claim: The GTF:Pol II occupancy ratios for all cases of GTF depletion are comparable to that observed prior to depletion.
source: Indeed, the GTF:Pol II occupancy ratios for all cases of GTF depletion are comparable to that observed prior to depletion (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The residual levels of transcription upon GTF depletion are due to incomplete depletion.
source: Thus, the residual levels of transcription are due to incomplete depletion
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GTF:Pol II occupancy ratios remain constant upon GTF depletion.

claim: All GTFs are required for Pol II transcription in vivo.
source: indicating that all GTFs are required for Pol II transcription in vivo
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that residual transcription is due to incomplete depletion rather than GTF-independent transcription.

claim: TBP occupancy levels at both continually expressed and heat-shock inducible genes are drastically reduced upon depletion of any GTF.
source: For all GTFs, TBP occupancy levels at both continually expressed (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and heat-shock inducible (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) genes are drastically reduced upon depletion.

claim: The TBP:Pol II and TBP:GTF occupancy ratios for all cases of GTF depletion are comparable to that observed prior to depletion and in the parental strain.
source: In addition, the TBP:Pol II and TBP:GTF occupancy ratios for all cases of GTF depletion are comparable to that observed prior to depletion and in the parental strain (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Each GTF is required for a stable PIC in vivo.
source: Thus, each GTF is required for a stable PIC in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TBP occupancy is drastically reduced upon depletion of any GTF.

claim: TBP is the only GTF that can independently and stably bind to DNA.
source: As TBP is the only GTF that can independently and stably bind to DNA (Buratowski et al., 1989)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Unlike the situation in vitro, partial PICs containing GTF subsets are very unstable in vivo.
source: these results indicate that, unlike the situation in vitro, partial PICs containing GTF subsets are very unstable in vivo
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TBP occupancy is drastically reduced upon depletion of any GTF.

claim: A previous report claimed the existence of partial PICs in response to a mild heat shock (37°C) based on altered GTF:GTF occupancy ratios.
source: Our results are in apparent contrast to a previous report claiming the existence of partial PICs in response to a mild heat shock (37°C) based on altered GTF:GTF occupancy ratios (Zanton and Pugh, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The altered occupancy ratios for the vast majority of the genes with apparent partial PICs reported by Zanton and Pugh (2006) are very modest.
source: However, in that report, the altered occupancy ratios for the vast majority of the genes with apparent partial PICs are very modest.
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of data from a prior study (Zanton and Pugh, 2006).

claim: Increased TFIIB:Pol II occupancy ratios in response to heat shock (39°C) were not observed at genes analyzed by Zanton and Pugh (2006).
source: To address this more directly, we measured the TFIIB and Pol II occupancies at several genes including those analyzed by Zanton and Pugh (2006). We did not observe increased TFIIB:Pol II occupancy ratios in response to heat shock (39°C) at any of these genes (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Partial PICs do not exist at appreciable levels in vivo, although their existence cannot be completely excluded.
source: Thus, our results suggest that partial PICs do not exist at appreciable levels in vivo, although their existence cannot be completely excluded.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing no evidence of partial PICs.

claim: Removal of uracil from the medium does not immediately eliminate intracellular uracil in ura3 mutant cells.
source: As removal of uracil from the medium does not immediately eliminate intracellular uracil (because ura3 cells require and hence contain uracil for growth prior to the removal)
evidence: This is based on logical inference about cellular metabolism.

claim: Uracil depletion causes metabolic mayhem.
source: As uracil depletion causes metabolic mayhem (Brauer et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Upon removal of uracil from the medium, cells grow at near-normal rates for about 2 hr and then show decreased growth with cessation at about 4 hr.
source: Upon removal of uracil from the medium, cells grow at near-normal rates for about 2 hr (using up the intracellular uracil) and then show decreased growth with cessation at about 4 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: With the exception of heat shock genes, TBP and Pol II occupancies at all promoters tested decrease over time upon uracil depletion.
source: With the exception of heat shock genes, TBP and Pol II occupancies at all promoters tested decrease over time
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: PIC and transcription levels are extremely low after 4 hr of uracil depletion.
source: and PIC and transcription (Pol II occupancy at coding regions) levels are extremely low after 4 hr
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The average TBP:Pol II occupancy ratio near the promoter decreases at intermediate times (15–60 min) of uracil depletion.
source: Interestingly, the average TBP:Pol II occupancy ratio near the promoter decreases at intermediate times (15–60 min) of uracil depletion (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The decreased TBP:Pol II ratio at intermediate times of uracil depletion is expected from Pol II buildup caused by reduced elongation due to decreased (but non-zero) UTP levels.
source: as would be expected from Pol II buildup caused by reduced elongation due to decreased (but non-zero) UTP levels
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation and knowledge of transcription elongation.

claim: At heat shock genes, TBP and Pol II occupancies sharply increase at early times of uracil depletion, presumably due to the stress response to uracil depletion.
source: At the heat shock genes, TBP and Pol II occupancies sharply increase at early times, presumably due to the stress response to uracil depletion
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and inferred from knowledge of stress responses.

claim: TBP and Pol II occupancies at heat shock genes drop to virtually undetectable levels after 2–4 hr of uracil depletion.
source: but they drop to virtually undetectable levels after 2–4 hr
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: TBP occupancy at Pol III and Pol I promoters is extremely low upon uracil depletion.
source: In addition, TBP occupancy at Pol III and Pol I promoters is also extremely low upon uracil depletion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The drastic drop in PIC levels upon uracil removal is unlikely to be due to growth arrest per se.
source: The drastic drop in PIC levels upon uracil removal is unlikely to be due to growth arrest per se, because depletion of Kin28 (Wong et al., 2014) or Taf1 (see below) only modestly reduces TBP and Pol II occupancy, even though cell growth is blocked.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other conditions that block growth but do not drastically reduce PIC levels.

claim: Leucine-depleted cells show a similar growth pattern as uracil-depleted cells with growth cessation at 4 hr.
source: Leucine-depleted cells show a similar growth pattern as uracil-depleted cells with growth cessation at 4 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Leucine-depleted cells do not show a drop in TBP and Pol II occupancy at all genes, although growth-inhibited genes are affected.
source: In contrast to the uracil-depleted cells, leucine-depleted cells do not show a drop in TBP and Pol II occupancy at all genes, although growth-inhibited genes are affected (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Leucine-depleted cells do not show early induction of PIC levels at heat shock genes.
source: In addition, leucine-depleted cells do not show early induction of PIC levels at heat shock genes, presumably because they do not undergo the same stress response
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and inferred from knowledge of stress responses.

claim: Leucine-depleted cells do not show increased Pol II:TBP ratios at intermediate times of leucine depletion.
source: nor do they show increased Pol II:TBP ratios at intermediate times of leucine depletion (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The differences between uracil- and leucine-depleted cells are consistent with transcriptional profiling experiments in auxotrophic cells grown in chemostats at various concentrations of the required metabolites.
source: The differences between uracil- and leucine-depleted cells are consistent with transcriptional profiling experiments in auxotrophic cells grown in chemostats at various concentrations of the required metabolites (Brauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The drastic and general drop in PIC levels upon uracil removal is due to the absence of UTP precursors.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the drastic and general drop in PIC levels upon uracil removal is due to the absence of UTP precursors.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations comparing uracil and leucine depletion.

source: FACT does not directly associate with promoters, but rather associates (directly or indirectly) with the elongation machinery after Pol II escapes from the promoter (Mason and Struhl, 2003).

claim: TFIIB occupancy at essentially all promoters is reduced to a comparable extent upon FACT depletion.

claim: FACT is important for PIC formation or stability.
source: indicating that FACT is important for PIC formation or stability

source: At 'SAGA-dependent' promoters (PMA1, CCW12), Taf1 levels are low, and Taf1 depletion has marginal effects on GTF occupancy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: The TBP:Taf1 occupancy ratio at SAGA-dependent promoters are far above those occurring in non-depleted cells upon Taf1 depletion.
source: As a consequence, the TBP:Taf1 occupancy ratio at these promoters are far above those occurring in non-depleted cells (Figure 7E).

claim: At 'TFIID-dependent' promoters with relatively high levels of Taf1 occupancy (RPL28 and RPS14B), GTF occupancy decreases upon Taf1 depletion.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: The TBP:Taf1 occupancy ratio at TFIID-dependent promoters is only slightly affected upon Taf1 depletion.
source: and the TBP:Taf1 occupancy ratio is only slightly affected (Figure 7E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Depletion of any individual GTF does not significantly alter the GTF:TBP or GTF:Pol II ratio.
source: In contrast and as shown above (Figure 2C), depletion of any individual GTF does not significantly alter the GTF:TBP or GTF:Pol II ratio.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TAF1 behaves differently than all GTFs and hence is selectively important but not required for Pol II transcription.
source: Thus, TAF1 behaves differently than all GTFs and hence is selectively important but not required for Pol II transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that substantial transcription and TBP occupancy occurs when Tafs are virtually absent from the promoter.

claim: Substantial transcription and TBP occupancy occurs when Tafs are virtually absent from the promoter.
source: However, our observation that substantial transcription and TBP occupancy occurs when Tafs are virtually absent from the promoter (i.e. a Taf1:TBP occupancy ratio of near zero) directly demonstrates the existence of a functional PIC lacking TAFs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: A functional PIC lacking TAFs exists.
source: directly demonstrates the existence of a functional PIC lacking TAFs
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that substantial transcription occurs when Tafs are virtually absent.

claim: In wild-type cells, the Taf1:TBP occupancy ratios vary between 0.2 and 1.0.
source: Importantly, in wild-type cells, the Taf1:TBP occupancy ratios vary between 0.2 and 1.0, indicating that TAFs (and hence TFIID) contribute to transcription at all promoters (Kuras et al., 2000)(Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and a citation to prior research.

claim: TAFs (and hence TFIID) contribute to transcription at all promoters.
source: indicating that TAFs (and hence TFIID) contribute to transcription at all promoters (Kuras et al., 2000)(Figure 7E)
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Taf1:TBP occupancy ratios vary between 0.2 and 1.0 in wild-type cells.

claim: Warfield et al. (2017) claimed that Taf-depletion resulted in 'similar transcription decreases for genes in the Taf-depleted, Taf-enriched, TATA-containing, and TATA-less gene classes'.
source: Our results are in apparent contrast to those of a recent study that claimed that Taf-depletion (via auxin-induced degradation) resulted in 'similar transcription decreases for genes in the Taf-depleted, Taf-enriched, TATA-containing, and TATA-less gene classes' (Warfield et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a citation to a prior study.

claim: The conclusion of Warfield et al. (2017) was based on analysis of all ~5000 yeast genes, most of which are transcribed at low or even background levels that prevent accurate measurements.
source: However, the conclusion of this other study was based on analysis of all ~5000 yeast genes, most of which are transcribed at low or even background levels that prevent accurate measurements.
evidence: This is a critical analysis of the methodology used in a prior study.

claim: Analysis of all ~5000 genes using the Taf1-depletion data shows a very modest difference between SAGA and TFIID-dependent promoters.
source: We performed a similar analysis of all ~5000 genes using the Taf1-depletion data presented here and confirmed a very modest difference between SAGA and TFIID-dependent promoters (Figure 7F; see 'all SAGA' and 'all TFIID').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: When the analysis is restricted to more actively transcribed genes, the distinction between 'active' SAGA and TFIID genes is clear upon Taf1 depletion.
source: When we restrict the analysis to more actively transcribed genes, for which Pol II occupancy levels are well above the background (i.e. the top 453 as shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 7A), the distinction between 'active' SAGA and TFIID genes is clear (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Among TFIID-affected genes, ribosomal protein genes are even more strongly affected by Taf1 depletion.
source: In addition, among TFIID-affected genes, ribosomal protein genes are even more strongly affected by Taf1 depletion (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Analysis of the same set of actively transcribed genes upon auxin-mediated depletion of Taf11 or Taf13 shows a clear distinction between SAGA and TFIID genes.
source: In accord with this result, analysis of the same set of actively transcribed genes upon auxin-mediated depletion of Taf11 or Taf13- (Warfield et al., 2017) shows a clear distinction between SAGA and TFIID genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and comparable to the Taf1-depletion data presented here.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and re-analysis of data from Warfield et al. (2017).

claim: The experimental results are completely consistent with those of Warfield et al. (2017).
source: Thus, our experimental results are completely consistent with those of Warfield et al. (2017)
evidence: This is inferred from re-analysis of data from Warfield et al. (2017).

claim: TFIID-specific Tafs are selectively important for transcription of TATA-less genes.
source: and they clearly demonstrate that TFIID-specific Tafs are selectively important for transcription of TATA-less genes
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential effects of Taf depletion on SAGA vs. TFIID genes.

claim: Every GTF is essential for Pol II transcription of essentially all genes in vivo.
source: Here, we show that every GTF is essential for Pol II transcription of essentially all genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: The limited amount of Pol II transcription observed upon GTF depletion is due to incomplete depletion, not GTF-independent transcription.
source: The limited amount of Pol II transcription observed upon GTF depletion is due to incomplete depletion, not GTF-independent transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GTF:Pol II occupancy ratios remain constant upon GTF depletion.

claim: The discrepancies between in vitro and in vivo results regarding GTF requirements are noteworthy.
source: While the basic observation is perhaps to be expected, the discrepancies between the in vitro and in vivo results are noteworthy.
evidence: This is a commentary on the comparison between in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The observation that TFIIE, TFIIF, and TFIIH are not required for in vitro transcription on negatively supercoiled templates is not relevant under physiological conditions.
source: While mechanistically interesting for understanding the transcription process, this observation is not relevant under physiological conditions, and it suggests that the DNA template is not negatively supercoiled in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The DNA template is not negatively supercoiled in vivo.
source: and it suggests that the DNA template is not negatively supercoiled in vivo
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TFIIE, TFIIF, and TFIIH are required in vivo but not on negatively supercoiled templates in vitro.

claim: The general requirement for TFIIA in vivo is unexpected.
source: The general requirement for TFIIA is unexpected.
evidence: This is a commentary on the findings regarding TFIIA.

claim: The ability of TFIIA to stabilize TBP binding to promoters is essential under physiological conditions.
source: This indicates that the ability of TFIIA to stabilize TBP binding to promoters is essential under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TFIIA is required for transcription in vivo.

claim: TAFs and Mediator contribute to PIC levels at most (and probably all) promoters, but they are not essential for PIC formation and hence are not GTFs.
source: Results presented here (see below) and elsewhere (Petrenko et al., 2017) indicate that although TAFs and Mediator contribute to PIC levels at most (and probably all) promoters, they are not essential for PIC formation and hence are not GTFs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in this manuscript and a citation to prior research.

claim: Transcriptionally active PICs can exist in the absence of TAFs or Mediator but not GTFs.
source: our direct analyses of factor occupancy here (Figure 7) and elsewhere (Petrenko et al., 2017) clearly indicate that transcriptionally active PICs can exist in the absence of TAFs or Mediator but not GTFs
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and a citation to prior research.

claim: The full complement of GTFs forms a PIC that is very stable in the absence of nucleotide precursors in vitro.
source: In vitro, the full complement of GTFs forms a PIC that is very stable in the absence of nucleotide precursors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from in vitro studies.

claim: Stepwise addition of GTFs results in a series of stable, partial PICs in vitro.
source: Moreover, stepwise addition of GTFs results in a series of stable, partial PICs (Buratowski et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cells have a mechanism(s) to prevent stable, transcriptionally inactive PICs despite the intrinsic ability of the GTFs to form them.
source: As such, cells have a mechanism(s) to prevent stable, transcriptionally inactive PICs despite the intrinsic ability of the GTFs to form them.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PICs are unstable in vivo under conditions where they are stable in vitro.

claim: The relative ratios of GTF occupancies are similar on a genome-wide level.
source: Consistent with this, the relative ratios of GTF occupancies are similar on a genome-wide level (Rhee and Pugh, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PICs are compositionally identical under the condition tested.
source: indicating that PICs are compositionally identical under the condition tested
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that relative ratios of GTF occupancies are similar genome-wide.

claim: The ts mutants used in earlier experiments may not completely inactivate TFIIB or Mediator.
source: The ts mutants used in these earlier experiments may not (and are unlikely to) completely inactivate TFIIB or Mediator, and promoter occupancy of these factors upon thermal inactivation was not assessed.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of prior experiments.

claim: Promoter occupancy of TFIIB and Mediator upon thermal inactivation was not assessed in earlier experiments.
source: and promoter occupancy of these factors upon thermal inactivation was not assessed
evidence: This is a statement about what was not done in prior experiments.

claim: Considerable mRNA remained from before the ts shift in earlier experiments, making it impossible to measure modest levels of transcription.
source: In addition, as transcription measurements relied on mRNA levels only 45 min after the ts shift, considerable mRNA remained from before the shift (i.e. wasn't degraded), thereby making it impossible to measure modest levels of transcription.
evidence: This is a critical analysis of the methodology used in prior experiments.

claim: Substantial transcription occurs in the Med17 ts (and anchor-away) strains.
source: Indeed, more recent experiments using Pol II occupancy as an assay indicate that substantial transcription occurs in the Med17 ts (and anchor-away) strains, and transcription and TBP occupancy is more efficient at TAF-dependent promoters (Petrenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Transcription and TBP occupancy is more efficient at TAF-dependent promoters in Med17 ts strains.
source: and transcription and TBP occupancy is more efficient at TAF-dependent promoters (Petrenko et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Metastable partial PICs might exist at earlier time points than 1 hr after GTF depletion.
source: However, as the Pol II occupancy measurements here are made 1 hr after GTF depletion, we cannot exclude the possibility that metastable partial PICs might exist at earlier time points.
evidence: This is speculation about a possibility that cannot be excluded by the current data.

claim: In wild-type cells, Mediator is part of the PIC.
source: In wild-type cells, Mediator is part of the PIC
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and prior research.

claim: Mediator dissociates from the PIC upon TFIIH-dependent phosphorylation of the C-terminal tail of Pol II, thereby permitting rapid promoter escape.
source: but it dissociates from the PIC upon TFIIH-dependent phosphorylation of the C-terminal tail of Pol II, thereby permitting rapid promoter escape (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mediator dissociation from the PIC is rapid (estimated life-time 1/8 s).
source: Mediator dissociation from the PIC is rapid (estimated life-time 1/8 s)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research (Wong et al., 2014).

claim: Mediator dissociation leaves behind a post-escape complex containing GTFs that is capable of re-initiation with a new Pol II molecule.
source: and it leaves behind a post-escape complex containing GTFs that is capable of re-initiation with a new Pol II molecule (Wong et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A Mediator-lacking PIC is competent for transcription in vivo, albeit at a lower level than a wild-type PIC.
source: A Mediator-lacking PIC is competent for transcription in vivo, albeit at a lower level than a wild-type PIC (Petrenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The PIC is extremely dynamic, both with respect to Mediator and to the instability of partial PICs.
source: Thus, the PIC is extremely dynamic, both with respect to Mediator and to the instability of partial PICs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations about Mediator dissociation and partial PIC instability.

claim: The lack of PICs in uracil-depleted cells does not simply reflect cessation of cell growth or metabolic mayhem.
source: The lack of PICs in uracil-depleted cells does not simply reflect cessation of cell growth or metabolic mayhem, because considerable PIC levels are observed upon depletion of Kin28, TAF1, or leucine, conditions in which cell growth is blocked.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of different conditions that block growth.

claim: The observation that general PIC loss is observed specifically during uracil depletion suggests that the effect is due to the elimination of UTP precursors.
source: The observation that general PIC loss is observed specifically during uracil depletion suggests that the effect is due to the elimination of UTP precursors.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations comparing uracil and leucine depletion.

claim: UTP limitation could affect PIC formation by leading to degradation, nuclear export, or an inactivating modification of a GTF.
source: In principle, UTP limitation could affect PIC formation by leading to degradation, nuclear export, or an inactivating modification of a GTF.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: UTP limitation could induce/activate a general inhibitory factor that blocks PIC formation or clears PICs from the promoter.
source: Alternatively, it could induce/activate a general inhibitory factor that blocks PIC formation or clears PICs from the promoter.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The fact that uracil depletion results in loss of Pol II and Pol III PICs suggests that the ultimate target of the signal might be something in common between these different transcription machineries, such as TBP or the common subunits of the RNA polymerases.
source: The fact that uracil depletion results in loss of Pol II and Pol III PICs suggests that the ultimate target of the signal might be something in common between these different transcription machineries, such as TBP or the common subunits of the RNA polymerases.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both Pol II and Pol III PICs are lost upon uracil depletion.

claim: There are TAF-containing (TFIID) and Taf-lacking forms of transcriptionally active TBP.
source: There are TAF-containing (TFIID) and Taf-lacking forms of transcriptionally active TBP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and citations to prior research.

claim: TFIID associates with promoters and contributes to transcription of all genes, but substantial transcription can occur in the absence of Tafs.
source: TFIID associates with promoters and contributes to transcription of all genes, but substantial transcription can occur in the absence of Tafs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The relative usage of the two TBP forms depends on the promoter, and occurs in a continuum.
source: The relative usage of the two TBP forms depends on the promoter, and occurs in a continuum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and prior research.

claim: The TFIID form is particularly important at TATA-lacking promoters, reflecting the importance of TAF:DNA contacts in the absence of a canonical TATA element.
source: The TFIID form is particularly important at TATA-lacking promoters, reflecting the importance of TAF:DNA contacts in the absence of a canonical TATA element (Verrijzer et al., 1994; Verrijzer et al., 1995; Oelgeschläger, et al., 1996; Burke and Kadonaga, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: The Taf-independent form typically requires a canonical TATA element for a stable interaction with TBP.
source: The Taf-independent form typically requires a canonical TATA element for a stable interaction with TBP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and prior research.

claim: The relative usage of the two TBP forms depends on the growth conditions, possible due to different levels of activator function which is linked to SAGA recruitment.
source: Lastly, it appears that the relative usage of the two forms depends on the growth conditions, possible due to different levels of activator function which is linked to SAGA recruitment.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations and prior research.

claim: Both TAF-containing and TAF-lacking TBP forms typically contribute (to various extents) to transcriptional activity of a given gene.
source: As both forms typically contribute (to various extents) to transcriptional activity of a given gene
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The terms 'TFIID-dependent' and 'TFIID-independent' (typically also called 'SAGA-dependent') genes are misleading.
source: the frequently used terms 'TFIID-dependent' and 'TFIID-independent' (typically also called 'SAGA-dependent') genes are misleading
evidence: This is a commentary on terminology based on the experimental findings.

claim: TATA elements are not the sole determinant of the relative usage of the two forms of transcriptional active TBP.
source: Furthermore, while TATA elements are less common in 'TFIID-dependent' genes as compared to 'TFIID-independent' genes, TATA elements are not the sole determinant of the relative usage of the two forms of transcriptional active TBP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and prior research.

claim: The multiple yeast Pol II machineries active at individual promoters are conceptually analogous to the multiple bacterial RNA polymerases that differ by the σ factor bound to the core enzyme and that can act at many individual promoters.
source: The multiple yeast Pol II machineries active at individual promoters are conceptually analogous to the multiple bacterial RNA polymerases that differ by the σ factor bound to the core enzyme and that can act at many individual promoters (Wade et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an analogy drawn from prior research.

claim: Anchor-away strains were constructed for subunits of TBP (Spt15), TFIIA (Toa1 and Toa2), TFIIB (Sua7), TFIIE (Tfa1 and Tfa2), TFIIF (Tfg1), TFIIH (Ssl1 and Ssl2), and Pol II (Rpb1).
source: To systematically study the role of GTFs and Pol II on transcription, we constructed anchor-away strains for subunits of TBP (Spt15), TFIIA (Toa1 and Toa2), TFIIB (Sua7), TFIIE (Tfa1 and Tfa2), TFIIF (Tfg1), TFIIH (Ssl1 and Ssl2), and Pol II (Rpb1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Taf1 depletion (via auxin-mediated proteolysis) in YPD medium caused a general 5-fold reduction in transcription.
source: Upon analysis of newly synthesized mRNA, Taf1 depletion (via auxin-mediated proteolysis) in YPD medium caused a general 5-fold reduction in transcription (Warfield et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Taf1 depletion in SC medium caused only a general 2-fold defect.
source: However, Taf1 depletion in SC medium caused only a general 2-fold defect (Warfield et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The difference in Taf1 function in YPD vs. SC medium is reminiscent of the difference in Mediator recruitment by activator proteins under these two conditions.
source: This difference in Taf1 function in YPD vs. SC medium is reminiscent of the difference in Mediator recruitment by activator proteins under these two conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: Activator function typically increases in sub-optimal growth conditions.
source: As activator function typically increases in sub-optimal growth conditions (Fan et al., 2006; Fan and Struhl, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The reduced activator function in YPD medium makes transcription more dependent on TFIID than SAGA.
source: we suggest that the reduced activator function in YPD medium makes transcription more dependent on TFIID than SAGA
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Taf1 depletion has a stronger effect in YPD than SC medium.

claim: The modest decrease in transcription in Taf1-depleted cells strongly argues against a general, GTF-like requirement for TFIID.
source: Importantly, in contrast to the dramatic decrease in transcription upon depletion of any individual GTF, the modest decrease in transcription in Taf1-depleted cells strongly argues against a general, GTF-like requirement for TFIID.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the effects of GTF vs. Taf1 depletion.

claim: The long-standing belief that TFIID is selectively important at different classes of promoters was based on two complementary findings.
source: The long-standing belief that TFIID is selectively important at different classes of promoters was based on two complementary findings.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical basis for a scientific view.

claim: The Taf1:GTF ratio is variable, strongly suggesting that there are TAF-containing and TAF-independent forms of transcriptionally active TBP.
source: First, unlike the constant GTF:GTF occupancy ratios at all promoters, the Taf1:GTF ratio is variable, strongly suggesting that there are TAF-containing and TAF-independent forms of transcriptionally active TBP (Kuras et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The different Taf1:GTF ratio could formally reflect differential crosslinking of TFIID at various promoters.
source: Formally, the different Taf1:GTF ratio could reflect differential crosslinking of TFIID at various promoters.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation.

claim: Genes showing higher relative levels of Tafs (and hence TFIID) show stronger reductions in transcription upon Taf depletion.
source: Second, genes showing higher relative levels of Tafs (and hence TFIID) show stronger reductions in transcription upon Taf depletion, thereby linking TFIID occupancy with TFIID-transcription.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Depletion of TAF1 affects 'TFIID-dependent' genes more strongly than 'SAGA-dependent' genes.
source: Our whole-genome analysis extends this observation and clearly demonstrates that depletion of TAF1 affects 'TFIID-dependent' genes more strongly than 'SAGA-dependent' genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The poor signal:noise of the vast majority of genes masked the TFIID vs. SAGA distinction in the analysis by Warfield et al. (2017).
source: In contrast, (Warfield et al., 2017) performed their analysis on all genes, and we suspect that the poor signal:noise of the vast majority of genes masked the TFIID vs. SAGA distinction.
evidence: This is speculation about why a prior study reached different conclusions.
